screens.title: System Resource Management with cgroups and systemd-slice
screens.narratorSegment: In advanced Linux administration you move beyond starting and stopping services to shaping how they consume resources. This chapter teaches the kernel feature called control groups, or cgroups, and how systemd maps slices, scopes, and service units into that hierarchy. You will see both transient techniques using systemd-run for on-the-fly limits and persistent approaches using. slice and. service unit files. We’ll emphasize practical configuration directives like MemoryMax, CPUQuota, IOWeight, and TasksMax, and show how to inspect cgroup state with systemd-cgtop, systemctl, and the cgroup filesystem. A concrete use case we’ll carry through the lesson is creating a limited-apps. slice, assigning a C P U burner service to it, and applying layered limits so the slice caps total resources while the service has its own tighter bounds. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes — for example, setting aggressive limits without testing — and show how to verify behavior so you avoid inadvertently killing services. By the end you’ll be able to design slices for groups of services, run one-off commands in transient scopes, and diagnose resource contention with the right systemd and cgroup tools.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Proper cgroup and systemd use prevents resource starvation, isolates workloads, and keeps a multi-service system stable and predictable.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Overview
System Resource Management
Control Groups and systemd slices for predictable service behavior

You will learn to allocate CPU, memory and I/O across services and transient processes, create persistent slice and service units, and diagnose contention using built-in tools.

In this lesson
•
Understand cgroup hierarchies and controllers (cpu, memory, blkio).
•
Create slices and assign services with layered limits.
•
Use systemd-run for transient testing and systemd-cgtop for diagnosis.
Key Idea

Map systemd units to cgroups so that resource directives become enforceable, inspectable kernel settings that protect system stability.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide hands-on work with cgroups and systemd. First, you will explain the purpose and hierarchy of control groups: what controllers exist, how the tree is structured, and why nesting matters. Second, you will use systemd-run to create transient scopes and services so you can test limits without creating persistent unit files; this is invaluable for quick experiments or isolating a suspected resource hog. Third, you will configure systemd slice, scope, and service units for persistent resource management, learning how slices group related services and how services inherit cgroup placement. Fourth, you will implement C P U, memory and input and output limits using systemd directives like MemoryMax, CPUQuota, IOWeight and TasksMax, and understand which directives belong in [Service] versus [Slice]. Each objective includes a concrete milestone: explain a cgroup hierarchy from /sys/fs/cgroup, run systemd-run with MemoryMax, create a slice unit, and set a service-level MemoryMax. Together these skills let you prevent resource starvation, isolate workloads, and diagnose contention. Practice each milestone in a safe test environment before applying limits to production services.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Skills
screens.narratorSegment: These applied objectives focus on the configuration directives and safe practices you must master. First, you will be able to implement resource limits for C P U using CPUShares and CPUQuota, and to enable CPUAccounting so you can measure usage. Second, you will learn to set MemoryMax, MemorySwapMax, and MemoryAccounting, and to reason about swap vs. physical memory when setting limits. Third, you will configure input and output limits with IOReadBandwidthMax, IOWriteBandwidthMax and IOWeight so storage-heavy services do not overwhelm disk bandwidth. Fourth, you will learn to set TasksMax to control process counts for a service, preventing fork bombs or runaway thread growth. Each skill includes a short practice: edit a. service or. slice file, reload systemd, and validate with systemctl show and /sys/fs/cgroup readings. Finally, remember the safety rule: always test limits in a non-production environment and start conservatively. This approach prevents accidental service failures and helps you tune limits incrementally.

screens.title: What are Control Groups (cgroups)?
screens.narratorSegment: Control Groups, or cgroups, are a kernel feature that let you group processes and apply resource policies to those groups. At its core, a cgroup is like a directory in a special filesystem where controllers — sometimes called subsystems — attach and enforce limits or account for usage. Think of the cgroup tree as a nested set of buckets: a parent bucket can set a total limit and child buckets receive a share of that total. This hierarchical model is important because it lets you impose both global constraints and per-service policies without modifying the application itself. For example, you can create a webapps slice that limits total memory to five gigabytes, and then assign each web service a smaller MemoryMax so no single service can exhaust the slice. A common misconception is that cgroups are only for containers; in reality the kernel applies cgroups to any processes, including system services and user sessions. Another misconception is that setting a single directive is always safe: aggressive MemoryMax or TasksMax values can kill services unexpectedly. A clear practice is to monitor first, apply conservative limits, and use transient testing with systemd-run to validate behavior. Reflect on how a nested cgroup lets you enforce organizational policies without changing processes themselves — why might a team prefer slices over per-service limits in a multi-tenant environment?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: cgroups are kernel-managed groups of processes arranged in a hierarchy that allow resource allocation and accounting.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › What are cgroups?
Control Groups — the kernel's grouping mechanism
Group processes, attach controllers, and enforce limits or accounting.
Hierarchy metaphor
Parent cgroups set aggregate limits; children inherit or get sub-allocations.
Controllers
Attach cpu, memory, blkio and others to apply resource policies.
Misconceptions
Not only for containers and don't set limits without testing.
Key Takeaway

Treat cgroups as nested resource buckets: plan parent limits first, then tune children conservatively, and verify with monitoring tools.

Concrete example
Imagine a shared server: create a webapps slice capped at 5G, then give each service a MemoryMax so no one service can starve the rest.
Inspecting cgroups
# List cgroupv2 tree (example)
ls /sys/fs/cgroup/
# Examine a service's control group path
systemctl show myservice.service -p ControlGroup
Check your understanding

Why prefer a slice for groups of related services rather than only setting individual service limits?

screens.title: slices, scopes, and services: how systemd maps to cgroups
screens.narratorSegment: systemd exposes three primary unit forms that map to cgroups: slices, scopes, and service units. Slices are the top-level grouping mechanism provided by systemd: they exist to collect other slices, scopes, and services and to set aggregate limits. Examples created by default include system. slice and user. slice. Scopes represent externally managed processes — things started by the shell or by external tools — and are often transient. You create a scope quickly with systemd-run --scope, and it is cleaned up when the process ends. Service units are the normal persistent services defined in. service files; they run under a slice by default and persist across reboots if enabled. A practical contrast: use a slice when you want to cap the combined resource consumption of related services; use a service-level directive when you want fine-grained limits for a particular daemon; use a scope for quick experiments or one-off constrained jobs. A common mistake is assigning conflicting limits at multiple levels without understanding inheritance: the kernel enforces both slice and service limits, so a service cannot exceed the slice’s cap. To validate placement and limits, inspect ControlGroup from systemctl show and read cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup. How would you decide whether to use a slice in a multi-tenant deployment versus service-level limits?

keyIdea.title: Unit mapping
keyIdea.text: Use slices for grouping, scopes for transient external processes, and services for persistent daemons; limits stack through the hierarchy.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Slices vs Scopes vs Services
Comparing unit types
Choose the unit form that matches lifecycle and grouping needs.
Slice (.slice)
Groups other units and sets aggregate limits. Use for logical service groups like webapp.slice.
Scope (.scope)
Transient representation of externally created processes; handy for one-off runs with systemd-run --scope.
Service (.service)
Persistent daemons which systemd manages directly; placed inside slices by default.
Key Takeaway

Pick slices to enforce group budgets, services for per-daemon tuning, and scopes for temporary experiments.

Concrete checks
# Show a service's control group path
systemctl show mycpuapp.service -p ControlGroup
# List transient scopes
systemctl list-units --type=scope
# Run a short test scope
sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M sleep 30
Misconception
A service's own MemoryMax overrides nothing; the kernel enforces both slice and service constraints, so both matter.

screens.title: Implementing CPU limits with systemd directives
screens.narratorSegment: Controlling C P U resources requires understanding two related but different directives: CPUShares and CPUQuota. CPUShares is a relative weight used by the scheduler: a higher value gives more C P U proportional share compared to siblings. The default is 1024; setting CPUShares to 256 gives lower relative priority. CPUQuota is an absolute throttle expressed as a percentage of a single C P U core or all CPUs, for example CPUQuota=50% limits the service to half a C P U worth of time. Use CPUAccounting=yes to enable usage measurement so you can reason about what to change. A practical pattern is to set a slice CPUQuota to cap total consumption, and then use CPUShares on services inside that slice to adjust relative priorities. A common mistake is confusing CPUShares and CPUQuota — CPUShares won't prevent a single process from using a whole core if nobody competes; CPUQuota enforces a hard limit. Example: in a high-priority. slice set CPUQuota=75% and in a service set CPUShares=256 for lower relative priority. After changing unit files always run systemctl daemon-reload and restart units, then observe with top, htop, or systemd-cgtop to verify the effective behavior. What would you observe in systemd-cgtop if a service is being C P U-throttled by CPUQuota?

keyIdea.title: CPU controls
keyIdea.text: Use CPUShares for relative weighting and CPUQuota for absolute throttling; enable accounting to measure results.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › CPU Limits
CPUQuota vs CPUShares
Absolute throttling vs relative priority; both useful depending on workload.
Example service fragment
[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/mycpuapp/cpu_burner.sh
CPUShares=256
CPUAccounting=yes
# Optional hard limit
# CPUQuota=25%
Checklist
  • Reload systemd after edits: systemctl daemon-reload
  • Restart the unit and observe CPU usage
  • Use systemd-cgtop to see per-cgroup CPU percentage
Key Takeaway

CPUShares tunes relative priority; CPUQuota enforces absolute limits. Use both with accounting to confirm effects.

Observing throttling
If CPUQuota is hit, systemd-cgtop and top will show reduced CPU usage and the service will not consume more than the quota over time.
# Real-time view
systemd-cgtop
# Show control group
systemctl show mycpuapp.service -p ControlGroup
Misconception
CPUShares alone does not cap CPU usage when no other contenders exist; it only sets relative priority under contention.

screens.title: Memory limits: MemoryMax, swap, and safety
screens.narratorSegment: Memory limits are among the most impactful cgroup settings because they can cause the kernel to kill a process if exceeded. MemoryMax sets an absolute cap on memory usage for a cgroup; MemorySwapMax limits combined R A M plus swap. Enabling MemoryAccounting=yes makes it easier to measure how much memory a unit consumes. When you set MemoryMax, the kernel enforces the cap and may trigger an OOM condition for that cgroup if usage exceeds the limit. Because of that risk, the common practice is to test MemoryMax with systemd-run in a transient scope before applying it to persistent services. For example, a service might run with MemoryMax=100M during a test to confirm it behaves, and later be raised to a production-appropriate value. A frequent error is to assume swap will always make a MemoryMax safe; with MemorySwapMax you must explicitly allow swap headroom or the cgroup might still be OOM-killed. After updating unit files remember to daemon-reload and inspect journalctl -u for cgroup memory messages. How would you verify whether a service was killed because it exceeded its MemoryMax? Memory limits: MemoryMax, swap, and safety means memorymax enforces absolute limits; test carefully and check journalctl for oom messages before applying to production.. In practical terms, setting absolute memory caps and understanding consequences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory safety
keyIdea.text: MemoryMax enforces absolute limits; test carefully and check journalctl for OOM messages before applying to production.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Memory Limits
MemoryMax and swap considerations
Absolute caps must be tested; swap behavior requires explicit configuration.
Example service limits
[Service]
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/data_processor.sh
MemoryAccounting=yes
MemoryMax=256M
MemorySwapMax=512M
Testing tip
Use sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M to validate behavior before updating a service unit.
Key Takeaway

Memory limits protect total system RAM but risk OOM if too low; always test and monitor journal messages for memory limit events.

Verifying OOM or limit hits
  • Check systemctl status for cgroup messages.
  • Inspect journalctl -u for "memory is above the limit" or OOM killer entries.
  • Read /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.current or memory.usage_in_bytes for live usage.
# Example checks
systemctl status myservice.service
journalctl -u myservice.service --since "5 minutes ago"
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/system.slice/myservice.service/memory.usage_in_bytes
Misconception
Assuming swap prevents OOM without setting MemorySwapMax and planning headroom is a risky shortcut.

screens.title: I/O and PIDs: preventing disk and process exhaustion
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond C P U and memory, disk input and output and process counts are common sources of contention. systemd exposes directives such as IOReadBandwidthMax and IOWriteBandwidthMax to limit throughput to a specific device, measured in bytes per second, and IOWeight to set a relative priority for block IO. Use BlockIOAccounting=yes to start accounting for block device usage. These controls help when a storage-bound job would otherwise saturate the device. Additionally, TasksMax caps the number of processes and threads a unit may spawn, useful to protect the system from forks or runaway thread creation. A typical pattern is to apply IOWeight or bandwidth limits to heavy batch jobs and set TasksMax to a conservative value for user-launched services. A common mistake is assuming IOWeight behaves like C P U shares; IOWeight is relative and device-specific, and bandwidth limits are absolute. To observe effects, run a dd or fio test under a constrained scope and monitor with systemd-cgtop or iostat. When would you prefer an absolute bandwidth cap over a relative IOWeight for a backup job that floods disks nightly? I/O and PIDs: preventing disk and process exhaustion means use bandwidth caps for absolute control and ioweight for relative prioritization; tasksmax protects against excessive process creation.. In practical terms, ioread/write limits, ioweight, and tasksmax. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: I/O & PIDs
keyIdea.text: Use bandwidth caps for absolute control and IOWeight for relative prioritization; TasksMax protects against excessive process creation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › I/O & PIDs
Prevent disk saturation
Use IORead/WriteBandwidthMax for absolute caps and IOWeight for relative prioritization.
Example slice I/O limits
[Slice]
# Limit reads to 10 megabytes per second on /dev/sda
IOReadBandwidthMax=/dev/sda 10M
IOWriteBandwidthMax=/dev/sda 10M
BlockIOAccounting=yes
TasksMax example
In a service: TasksMax=100 limits processes/threads spawned by the unit.
Key Takeaway

Use bandwidth caps when you need firm device limits; use IOWeight when you want the kernel to balance contention fairly across cgroups.

Testing I/O limits
Run a dd to generate load and observe cgroup behavior.
# Example transient test
sudo systemd-run --scope -p IOReadBandwidthMax=/dev/sda:10M dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1000
# Monitor
systemd-cgtop
Misconception
IOWeight does not fix absolute bandwidth issues; bandwidth caps are needed when you must guarantee a maximum throughput.

screens.title: Transient resource testing with systemd-run
screens.narratorSegment: systemd-run is a powerful command for creating transient units so you can apply resource directives on the fly. Use the --scope option when you want the command to become a scope unit tied to the current process; this scope is automatically removed when the process exits. For example, to test a memory limit run sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M /usr/bin/some-script. This runs the script in its own cgroup, enforcing MemoryMax only for that invocation. systemd-run is ideal for experiments, load testing, or isolating a problematic script before creating a persistent service unit. After starting a transient scope, list units of type scope to find its name, then inspect cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup to confirm the kernel applied the directive. A typical workflow is: pick a conservative limit, run systemd-run, observe with systemd-cgtop and journalctl, adjust, and only then write unit files in /etc/systemd/system. keyIdea.title: Transient testing
keyIdea.text: Use systemd-run --scope with -p directives to validate limits before committing persistent units.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Transient testing
Run a command with limits
Use systemd-run --scope to create a short-lived cgroup and apply -p directives.
# Example: limit memory and CPU for a short job
sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M -p CPUQuota=10% /bin/bash -c "dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1000"

# Find the scope and monitor
systemctl list-units --type=scope
systemd-cgtop
Workflow
Choose limits → run transient scope → observe → tweak → create persistent unit.
Key Takeaway

Transient scopes let you experiment safely; they avoid cluttering /etc/systemd/system with temporary unit files.

Example scenario
You suspect a data_processor script uses too much memory. Run it with MemoryMax=256M in a scope, monitor with systemd-cgtop, and inspect journalctl for memory messages. If safe, then create a service unit.
Misconception
Transient scopes are not invisible; they are managed units you can list and inspect like any other systemd unit.

screens.title: Creating a persistent slice and assigning a service
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a persistent slice and assigning services shows the power of hierarchical resource policies. Begin by writing a. slice unit in /etc/systemd/system. In the example from the chapter we create limited-apps. slice with MemoryMax=500M and CPUQuota=50%. That sets the group cap. Next create a mycpuapp. service that sets Slice=limited-apps. slice in its [Unit] section and includes service-level limits like CPUShares=256, MemoryMax=100M, and TasksMax=5. After placing both unit files run systemctl daemon-reload and enable or start the service. Verification steps include systemctl status to see cgroup assignments, reading cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup to confirm memory and C P U quotas, and using systemd-cgtop to watch runtime usage. Remember slices need not be explicitly started; starting services in them creates the slice. A common oversight is forgetting to daemon-reload or misplacing the Slice= directive, which keeps the service in system. slice instead of the intended custom slice. Follow the sequence: create files, reload, enable/start, and then inspect both systemctl and the cgroup filesystem to confirm limits are active and correctly inherited. Creating a persistent slice and assigning a service means create .slice and .service units, reload systemd, start services, and confirm with control group paths and cgroup files.. In practical terms, step-by-step unit files and verification commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Persistent configuration
keyIdea.text: Create .slice and .service units, reload systemd, start services, and confirm with control group paths and cgroup files.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Create slice & service
Slice unit example
# /etc/systemd/system/limited-apps.slice
[Unit]
Description=Limited Applications Slice

[Slice]
CPUQuota=50%
MemoryMax=500M
Service unit example
# /etc/systemd/system/mycpuapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My CPU Intensive Application
Slice=limited-apps.slice

[Service]
User=nobody
ExecStart=/opt/mycpuapp/cpu_burner.sh
CPUShares=256
MemoryMax=100M
TasksMax=5
Restart=on-failure
Verification steps
  1. sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  2. sudo systemctl enable mycpuapp.service
  3. sudo systemctl start mycpuapp.service
  4. systemctl show mycpuapp.service -p ControlGroup
  5. cat /sys/fs/cgroup/.../memory.current and cpu files to confirm
Common mistake
Forgetting Slice= keeps the service in system.slice, meaning your intended group limits won't apply.
Key Takeaway

Use slice units to define group budgets and assign services to them with Slice= so limits are applied hierarchically and predictably.

screens.title: Diagnosing resource contention and OOM events
screens.narratorSegment: When resource contention occurs you must quickly identify which cgroup or service consumed resources and whether it hit a configured limit. Start with systemd-cgtop for a live, hierarchical view: it shows C P U, memory and input and output consumption per cgroup so you can spot high consumers. Next, inspect systemctl status for immediate hints and use journalctl -u to search for messages like 'memory is above the limit' or OOM killer events. For direct inspection, read cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup for the relevant controller and unit path. For example, cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/system. slice/mywebapp. service/memory. usage_in_bytes shows current memory usage. A practical diagnosis workflow is: monitor with systemd-cgtop to find the candidate, check systemctl and journalctl for limit hits, and then read cgroup metrics to confirm exact usage numbers. A common oversight is adjusting limits before understanding whether the service is truly misbehaving; first monitor, then tune. Also remember journal entries will often show why a service was killed — look for cgroup memory messages rather than assuming generic instability. After diagnosing, apply conservative limit changes and retest with transient scopes or in a staging environment.

keyIdea.title: Diagnosis workflow
keyIdea.text: Monitor with systemd-cgtop, verify with systemctl/journalctl, and confirm with cgroup filesystem reads for responsible tuning.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Diagnose contention
Quick triage steps
  1. Run systemd-cgtop to spot heavy cgroups.
  2. Inspect systemctl status for cgroup-related messages.
  3. Use journalctl -u to find OOM or memory-limit entries.
  4. Read cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup for exact metrics.
Example checks
systemd-cgtop
systemctl status mywebapp.service
journalctl -u mywebapp.service --since "10 minutes ago"
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/system.slice/mywebapp.service/memory.usage_in_bytes
Interpretation tips
  • Look for messages that explicitly mention cgroup memory limits or OOM.
  • Compare slice totals vs individual services to see which child consumes the budget.
  • Use timestamps in journalctl to correlate spikes with service actions.
Key Takeaway

Diagnose first with monitoring, then adjust limits conservatively and retest with transient scopes to avoid accidental outages.

screens.title: How systemd translates unit directives into cgroup settings
screens.narratorSegment: systemd acts as the user-space orchestrator that converts unit file directives into cgroup configuration the kernel enforces. When you set MemoryMax= or CPUQuota= in a unit, systemd writes the corresponding values into the cgroup filesystem or uses the cgroup v2 unified interface so the kernel can enforce limits and record accounting. Every started unit is placed into a control group whose path you can discover via systemctl show -p ControlGroup. Understanding this mapping matters when you debug behavior: systemd's directives are not merely annotations but active changes to kernel state. For example, setting MemoryMax on a service results in a memory. max change in the cgroup v2 filesystem. A pitfall is assuming the directive applies immediately to all child processes; while systemd creates the cgroup and adds processes, race conditions can occur if processes spawn before systemd assigns them. For persistent services systemctl start ensures systemd places processes correctly; for external processes you may need systemd-run --scope. As you design policies, remember that slices provide aggregate enforcement and services provide per-unit limits. Reflect on how this translation gives you programmatic control over kernel resource enforcement without touching application code.

keyIdea.title: Translation layer
keyIdea.text: systemd converts unit directives into cgroup settings the kernel enforces, so unit configuration directly affects kernel cgroup state.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › systemd → kernel
Unit directive to cgroup mapping
systemd writes directives into the cgroup filesystem so the kernel enforces them.
Examples of mapping
  • MemoryMax → memory.max (cgroup v2)
  • CPUQuota → cpu.max or equivalent throttle
  • IO* directives → block I/O controller entries
Race note

Ensure systemd launches and places processes in the intended cgroup; externally started processes may require systemd-run --scope to be managed correctly.

Verify kernel state
# Show control group path
systemctl show myservice.service -p ControlGroup
# Inspect cgroup files
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/myservice.service/memory.max
Key Takeaway

Unit directives are actionable: systemd applies them to the kernel cgroup interface so your configuration becomes enforceable system policy.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Create script, write slice and service units, reload systemd, start units, and verify with systemd-cgtop and cgroup filesystem reads.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Lab: limited-apps
Step 1 — Create CPU burner script
sudo tee /opt/mycpuapp/cpu_burner.sh > /dev/null <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "Starting CPU burner..."
while true; do
  : $((i++))
done
EOF
sudo chmod +x /opt/mycpuapp/cpu_burner.sh
Step 2 — Create slice and service files
# limited-apps.slice
[Unit]
Description=Limited Applications Slice

[Slice]
CPUQuota=50%
MemoryMax=500M

# mycpuapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My CPU Intensive Application
Slice=limited-apps.slice

[Service]
User=nobody
ExecStart=/opt/mycpuapp/cpu_burner.sh
CPUShares=256
MemoryMax=100M
TasksMax=5
Restart=on-failure
Step 3 — Reload, enable, start
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable mycpuapp.service
sudo systemctl start mycpuapp.service

# Verify
systemctl show mycpuapp.service -p ControlGroup
systemd-cgtop
If things fail
Check journalctl -u mycpuapp.service for cgroup memory or OOM messages and confirm the service's cgroup path under /sys/fs/cgroup.
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence and verify after each change. This prevents accidental misplacement of units or forgetting to apply new cgroup settings.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Remember three central ideas: first, cgroups are the kernel mechanism that group processes and enforce resource policies; treat them as hierarchical buckets where parents cap totals and children receive shares or limits. Second, systemd maps slices, scopes, and services directly into cgroups so unit directives like MemoryMax and CPUQuota become kernel-enforced settings; design slices for group budgets and services for per-daemon tuning. Third, use transient testing with systemd-run and monitoring with systemd-cgtop and journalctl before applying persistent limits. Always test conservatively, inspect cgroup files to verify kernel settings, and read journal messages to detect OOM or cgroup limit hits. These habits let you safely enforce predictable resource behavior and recover quickly if limits are too strict. fullNarratorScript:
In advanced Linux administration you move beyond starting and stopping services to shaping how they consume resources. This chapter teaches the kernel feature called control groups, or cgroups, and how systemd maps slices, scopes, and service units into that hierarchy. You will see both transient techniques using systemd-run for on-the-fly limits and persistent approaches using. slice and. service unit files. We’ll emphasize practical configuration directives like MemoryMax, CPUQuota, IOWeight, and TasksMax, and show how to inspect cgroup state with systemd-cgtop, systemctl, and the cgroup filesystem. A concrete use case we’ll carry through the lesson is creating a limited-apps. slice, assigning a C P U burner service to it, and applying layered limits so the slice caps total resources while the service has its own tighter bounds. Along the way I’ll highlight common mistakes — for example, setting aggressive limits without testing — and show how to verify behavior so you avoid inadvertently killing services. By the end you’ll be able to design slices for groups of services, run one-off commands in transient scopes, and diagnose resource contention with the right systemd and cgroup tools.

These objectives guide hands-on work with cgroups and systemd. First, you will explain the purpose and hierarchy of control groups: what controllers exist, how the tree is structured, and why nesting matters. Second, you will use systemd-run to create transient scopes and services so you can test limits without creating persistent unit files; this is invaluable for quick experiments or isolating a suspected resource hog. Third, you will configure systemd slice, scope, and service units for persistent resource management, learning how slices group related services and how services inherit cgroup placement. Fourth, you will implement C P U, memory and input and output limits using systemd directives like MemoryMax, CPUQuota, IOWeight and TasksMax, and understand which directives belong in [Service] versus [Slice]. Each objective includes a concrete milestone: explain a cgroup hierarchy from /sys/fs/cgroup, run systemd-run with MemoryMax, create a slice unit, and set a service-level MemoryMax. Together these skills let you prevent resource starvation, isolate workloads, and diagnose contention. Practice each milestone in a safe test environment before applying limits to production services.

These applied objectives focus on the configuration directives and safe practices you must master. First, you will be able to implement resource limits for C P U using CPUShares and CPUQuota, and to enable CPUAccounting so you can measure usage. Second, you will learn to set MemoryMax, MemorySwapMax, and MemoryAccounting, and to reason about swap vs. physical memory when setting limits. Third, you will configure input and output limits with IOReadBandwidthMax, IOWriteBandwidthMax and IOWeight so storage-heavy services do not overwhelm disk bandwidth. Fourth, you will learn to set TasksMax to control process counts for a service, preventing fork bombs or runaway thread growth. Each skill includes a short practice: edit a. service or. slice file, reload systemd, and validate with systemctl show and /sys/fs/cgroup readings. Finally, remember the safety rule: always test limits in a non-production environment and start conservatively. This approach prevents accidental service failures and helps you tune limits incrementally.

Control Groups, or cgroups, are a kernel feature that let you group processes and apply resource policies to those groups. At its core, a cgroup is like a directory in a special filesystem where controllers — sometimes called subsystems — attach and enforce limits or account for usage. Think of the cgroup tree as a nested set of buckets: a parent bucket can set a total limit and child buckets receive a share of that total. This hierarchical model is important because it lets you impose both global constraints and per-service policies without modifying the application itself. For example, you can create a webapps slice that limits total memory to five gigabytes, and then assign each web service a smaller MemoryMax so no single service can exhaust the slice. A common misconception is that cgroups are only for containers; in reality the kernel applies cgroups to any processes, including system services and user sessions. Another misconception is that setting a single directive is always safe: aggressive MemoryMax or TasksMax values can kill services unexpectedly. A clear practice is to monitor first, apply conservative limits, and use transient testing with systemd-run to validate behavior. Reflect on how a nested cgroup lets you enforce organizational policies without changing processes themselves — why might a team prefer slices over per-service limits in a multi-tenant environment?

systemd exposes three primary unit forms that map to cgroups: slices, scopes, and service units. Slices are the top-level grouping mechanism provided by systemd: they exist to collect other slices, scopes, and services and to set aggregate limits. Examples created by default include system. slice and user. slice. Scopes represent externally managed processes — things started by the shell or by external tools — and are often transient. You create a scope quickly with systemd-run --scope, and it is cleaned up when the process ends. Service units are the normal persistent services defined in. service files; they run under a slice by default and persist across reboots if enabled. A practical contrast: use a slice when you want to cap the combined resource consumption of related services; use a service-level directive when you want fine-grained limits for a particular daemon; use a scope for quick experiments or one-off constrained jobs. A common mistake is assigning conflicting limits at multiple levels without understanding inheritance: the kernel enforces both slice and service limits, so a service cannot exceed the slice’s cap. To validate placement and limits, inspect ControlGroup from systemctl show and read cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup. How would you decide whether to use a slice in a multi-tenant deployment versus service-level limits?

Controlling C P U resources requires understanding two related but different directives: CPUShares and CPUQuota. CPUShares is a relative weight used by the scheduler: a higher value gives more C P U proportional share compared to siblings. The default is 1024; setting CPUShares to 256 gives lower relative priority. CPUQuota is an absolute throttle expressed as a percentage of a single C P U core or all CPUs, for example CPUQuota=50% limits the service to half a C P U worth of time. Use CPUAccounting=yes to enable usage measurement so you can reason about what to change. A practical pattern is to set a slice CPUQuota to cap total consumption, and then use CPUShares on services inside that slice to adjust relative priorities. A common mistake is confusing CPUShares and CPUQuota — CPUShares won't prevent a single process from using a whole core if nobody competes; CPUQuota enforces a hard limit. Example: in a high-priority. slice set CPUQuota=75% and in a service set CPUShares=256 for lower relative priority. After changing unit files always run systemctl daemon-reload and restart units, then observe with top, htop, or systemd-cgtop to verify the effective behavior. What would you observe in systemd-cgtop if a service is being C P U-throttled by CPUQuota?

Memory limits are among the most impactful cgroup settings because they can cause the kernel to kill a process if exceeded. MemoryMax sets an absolute cap on memory usage for a cgroup; MemorySwapMax limits combined R A M plus swap. Enabling MemoryAccounting=yes makes it easier to measure how much memory a unit consumes. When you set MemoryMax, the kernel enforces the cap and may trigger an OOM condition for that cgroup if usage exceeds the limit. Because of that risk, the common practice is to test MemoryMax with systemd-run in a transient scope before applying it to persistent services. For example, a service might run with MemoryMax=100M during a test to confirm it behaves, and later be raised to a production-appropriate value. A frequent error is to assume swap will always make a MemoryMax safe; with MemorySwapMax you must explicitly allow swap headroom or the cgroup might still be OOM-killed. After updating unit files remember to daemon-reload and inspect journalctl -u for cgroup memory messages. How would you verify whether a service was killed because it exceeded its MemoryMax? Beyond C P U and memory, disk input and output and process counts are common sources of contention. systemd exposes directives such as IOReadBandwidthMax and IOWriteBandwidthMax to limit throughput to a specific device, measured in bytes per second, and IOWeight to set a relative priority for block IO. Use BlockIOAccounting=yes to start accounting for block device usage. These controls help when a storage-bound job would otherwise saturate the device. Additionally, TasksMax caps the number of processes and threads a unit may spawn, useful to protect the system from forks or runaway thread creation. A typical pattern is to apply IOWeight or bandwidth limits to heavy batch jobs and set TasksMax to a conservative value for user-launched services. A common mistake is assuming IOWeight behaves like C P U shares; IOWeight is relative and device-specific, and bandwidth limits are absolute. To observe effects, run a dd or fio test under a constrained scope and monitor with systemd-cgtop or iostat. When would you prefer an absolute bandwidth cap over a relative IOWeight for a backup job that floods disks nightly? systemd-run is a powerful command for creating transient units so you can apply resource directives on the fly. Use the --scope option when you want the command to become a scope unit tied to the current process; this scope is automatically removed when the process exits. For example, to test a memory limit run sudo systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=50M /usr/bin/some-script. This runs the script in its own cgroup, enforcing MemoryMax only for that invocation. systemd-run is ideal for experiments, load testing, or isolating a problematic script before creating a persistent service unit. After starting a transient scope, list units of type scope to find its name, then inspect cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup to confirm the kernel applied the directive. A typical workflow is: pick a conservative limit, run systemd-run, observe with systemd-cgtop and journalctl, adjust, and only then write unit files in /etc/systemd/system. A common misconception is that transient units cannot be monitored; they can — systemctl list-units --type=scope and systemd-cgtop both reveal transient scope usage. Try this technique first in a non-production environment to avoid surprises. Creating a persistent slice and assigning services shows the power of hierarchical resource policies. Begin by writing a. slice unit in /etc/systemd/system. In the example from the chapter we create limited-apps. slice with MemoryMax=500M and CPUQuota=50%. That sets the group cap. Next create a mycpuapp. service that sets Slice=limited-apps. slice in its [Unit] section and includes service-level limits like CPUShares=256, MemoryMax=100M, and TasksMax=5. After placing both unit files run systemctl daemon-reload and enable or start the service. Verification steps include systemctl status to see cgroup assignments, reading cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup to confirm memory and C P U quotas, and using systemd-cgtop to watch runtime usage. Remember slices need not be explicitly started; starting services in them creates the slice. A common oversight is forgetting to daemon-reload or misplacing the Slice= directive, which keeps the service in system. slice instead of the intended custom slice. Follow the sequence: create files, reload, enable/start, and then inspect both systemctl and the cgroup filesystem to confirm limits are active and correctly inherited. When resource contention occurs you must quickly identify which cgroup or service consumed resources and whether it hit a configured limit. Start with systemd-cgtop for a live, hierarchical view: it shows C P U, memory and input and output consumption per cgroup so you can spot high consumers. Next, inspect systemctl status for immediate hints and use journalctl -u to search for messages like 'memory is above the limit' or OOM killer events. For direct inspection, read cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup for the relevant controller and unit path. For example, cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/system. slice/mywebapp. service/memory. usage_in_bytes shows current memory usage. A practical diagnosis workflow is: monitor with systemd-cgtop to find the candidate, check systemctl and journalctl for limit hits, and then read cgroup metrics to confirm exact usage numbers. A common oversight is adjusting limits before understanding whether the service is truly misbehaving; first monitor, then tune. Also remember journal entries will often show why a service was killed — look for cgroup memory messages rather than assuming generic instability. After diagnosing, apply conservative limit changes and retest with transient scopes or in a staging environment.

systemd acts as the user-space orchestrator that converts unit file directives into cgroup configuration the kernel enforces. When you set MemoryMax= or CPUQuota= in a unit, systemd writes the corresponding values into the cgroup filesystem or uses the cgroup v2 unified interface so the kernel can enforce limits and record accounting. Every started unit is placed into a control group whose path you can discover via systemctl show -p ControlGroup. Understanding this mapping matters when you debug behavior: systemd's directives are not merely annotations but active changes to kernel state. For example, setting MemoryMax on a service results in a memory. max change in the cgroup v2 filesystem. A pitfall is assuming the directive applies immediately to all child processes; while systemd creates the cgroup and adds processes, race conditions can occur if processes spawn before systemd assigns them. For persistent services systemctl start ensures systemd places processes correctly; for external processes you may need systemd-run --scope. As you design policies, remember that slices provide aggregate enforcement and services provide per-unit limits. Reflect on how this translation gives you programmatic control over kernel resource enforcement without touching application code.

Remember three central ideas: first, cgroups are the kernel mechanism that group processes and enforce resource policies; treat them as hierarchical buckets where parents cap totals and children receive shares or limits. Second, systemd maps slices, scopes, and services directly into cgroups so unit directives like MemoryMax and CPUQuota become kernel-enforced settings; design slices for group budgets and services for per-daemon tuning. Third, use transient testing with systemd-run and monitoring with systemd-cgtop and journalctl before applying persistent limits. Always test conservatively, inspect cgroup files to verify kernel settings, and read journal messages to detect OOM or cgroup limit hits. These habits let you safely enforce predictable resource behavior and recover quickly if limits are too strict.
